topics.name: Variation: do organisms create exact copies?

questions.title: Where does implantation happen?
questions.text: In human beings, the implantation of the fertilised egg takes place in which part of the female reproductive system?
opts: Oviduct
Cervix
Uterus
Vagina
steps: ① Egg released by the ovary enters the oviduct
② Fertilisation happens in the oviduct
③ The zygote divides and moves down to the uterus
④ It embeds in the thick uterine lining: implantation
∴ Uterus → (c)
questions.remember: Fertilisation in the oviduct (fallopian tube); implantation in the uterus wall; the placenta then supplies food and oxygen to the embryo.
questions.trap: Picking the oviduct: that's where FERTILISATION happens, not implantation.
questions.tryit: Which tissue links the embryo to the mother's blood?

questions.title: How does Spirogyra reproduce?
questions.text: Spirogyra, despite being a multi-cellular organism, still shows a simple reproductive method. Select the correct option with regard to reproduction in Spirogyra:
opts: Asexual reproduction by division of cells into two cells
Sexual reproduction by division of cells into many cells
Asexual reproduction by breaking up of Spirogyra filaments into smaller parts
Sexual reproduction by the formation of gametes after meiosis
steps: ① Spirogyra: a filament of many similar cells
② When mature, the filament simply breaks into pieces
③ Each piece grows into a new filament
④ One parent, no gametes ⟹ asexual: fragmentation
∴ Breaking up of filaments → (c)
questions.ans: Option (c) Asexual reproduction by breaking up of Spirogyra filaments into smaller parts
questions.remember: Fragmentation: the body breaks into pieces and each grows into a new organism (Spirogyra). Regeneration: specialised cells regrow lost parts (Planaria, Hydra).
questions.trap: Picking (a) 'division into two cells': that's binary fission of single cells like Amoeba, not a multicellular filament.
questions.tryit: Name an organism that reproduces by multiple fission.

questions.title: Why chromosome numbers stay constant
questions.text: The number of chromosomes in parents and offspring of a particular species undergoing sexual reproduction remains constant due to:
opts: doubling of chromosomes after zygote formation.
halving of chromosomes after zygote formation.
doubling of chromosomes before gamete formation.
halving of chromosomes at the time of gamete formation.
steps: ① Body cells: 46 chromosomes (humans)
② Gametes are made by halving: 23 each
③ Sperm (23) + egg (23) ⟹ zygote 46
④ Back to the full number every generation
∴ Halving at gamete formation → (d)
questions.ans: Option (d) halving of chromosomes at the time of gamete formation
questions.remember: Gametes carry half the chromosomes (one set). Fusion of two gametes restores the full number in the zygote, so it stays constant across generations.
questions.trap: Picking (b): if chromosomes halved AFTER the zygote formed, every generation would still start doubled. The halving must come before, in the gametes.
questions.tryit: How many chromosomes are there in a human sperm?

questions.title: From pollination to seed
questions.text: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of events of sexual reproduction in a flower?
opts: Pollination, Fertilization, Seed, Embryo
Seed, Embryo, Fertilization, Pollination
Seed, Plant, Flower, Pollination, Fertilization
Pollination, Fertilization, Embryo, Seed
steps: ① Pollination: pollen reaches the stigma
② Fertilisation: male gamete fuses with the egg ⟹ zygote
③ Zygote develops into the embryo
④ The ovule, with its embryo, becomes the seed
∴ Pollination → fertilisation → embryo → seed → (d)
questions.remember: After fertilisation: zygote → embryo, ovule → seed, ovary → fruit; petals, sepals and stamens wither.
questions.trap: Picking (a): the embryo forms INSIDE the ovule first, and then the ovule becomes the seed. Embryo comes before seed.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 7 · Section 7.3.3 Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
questions.tryit: What does the ovary develop into after fertilisation?

questions.title: Assertion–Reason: variation in asexual reproduction
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Variations are not often seen in offsprings produced by asexual reproduction.
Reason (R): DNA molecule generated by replication is not similar to the original DNA.
opts: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
steps: ① Asexual: one parent, DNA copied ⟹ offspring very similar ✓ A true
② DNA copying is very accurate
③ Copies are SIMILAR to the original, with only tiny errors
④ So 'not similar' is wrong ⟹ R false
∴ A true, R false → (c)
questions.ans: Option (c) A is true, but R is false
questions.remember: DNA replication is reliable but not perfect: copies are similar to the original with minor variations. Sexual reproduction creates far more variation.
questions.trap: Accepting R because 'copying errors exist'. R says the copy is NOT SIMILAR, which is false: it is similar, with small changes.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 7 · Section 7.1 Do organisms create exact copies of themselves?
questions.tryit: Why is variation useful for a species?
questions.tryans: It helps some individuals survive changes in the environment

questions.title: The male reproductive system (5 marks)
questions.text:
(i) Name an organ that helps in the formation of male germ cells in humans and mention the condition that favours their formation.
(ii) Write the pathway followed to deliver male germ cells to the site of fertilisation.
(iii) Mention the main physical feature of the male germ cell that helps it move towards the female germ cell.
steps: ① (i) Testes make sperms
② They lie in the scrotum, outside the abdomen: 2–2.5 °C cooler, which sperm need
③ (ii) Testes → vas deferens → urethra (glands add fluid)
④ Into the vagina → cervix → uterus → oviduct (site of fertilisation)
⑤ (iii) Sperm have a long tail to swim towards the egg
∴ Testes · cooler temperature · pathway · long tail
questions.ans: (i) Testes; a temperature 2–2.5 °C lower than body temperature (scrotum outside the abdomen) · (ii) testes → vas deferens → urethra → vagina → cervix → uterus → oviduct · (iii) a long tail
questions.remember: Seminal vesicles and the prostate gland add fluid that nourishes and carries the sperm. Testes also secrete testosterone.
questions.trap: (i): writing 'body temperature'. Sperm form at a LOWER temperature: that's why the testes hang outside in the scrotum.
questions.ncert: NCERT Ch 7 · Section 7.3.4 (male reproductive system, Fig. 7.10)
questions.tryit: Name the hormone made by the testes.

questions.title: Sugarcane and vegetative propagation (5 marks)
questions.text:
(i) Sugarcane does not produce seeds, so name the process through which it will be able to reproduce.
(ii) List any two advantages of this method.
(iii) Besides sugarcane, give two more examples of plants that reproduce by this method.
(iv) Why is regeneration not possible in all types of animals?
steps: ① (i) Vegetative propagation: stem pieces with nodes are planted
② (ii) Plants grow faster and bear flowers and fruits earlier
③ All new plants are identical to the parent (desired traits kept)
④ (iii) Banana, rose, grapes, potato, Bryophyllum
⑤ (iv) Complex animals have specialised cells, tissues and organs
⑥ They can't regrow a whole body from a piece
∴ Vegetative propagation · faster, identical · examples · complexity
questions.ans: (i) Vegetative propagation (stem cuttings) · (ii) faster flowering/fruiting; offspring identical to the parent · (iii) e.g. banana, rose, grapes, potato, Bryophyllum · (iv) complex animals have highly specialised cells and organs, so a piece can't regrow the whole body
questions.remember: Vegetative propagation lets seedless plants (banana, sugarcane, orange) reproduce and keeps desirable traits. Simple animals like Planaria and Hydra regenerate.
questions.trap: (iv): saying 'animals don't have cells that divide'. The point is SPECIALISATION: complex bodies have organs that can't be rebuilt from one piece.
questions.tryans: Buds on the margins of its leaves grow into new plants
